content: Cryoprecipitate is a blood product derived from plasma. Each 15 mL unit of cryoprecipitate contains approximately 100 units of factor VIII, 250 mg of fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, factor XIII, and fibronectin. It is important to note that according to established standards, each bag of cryoprecipitate must contain a minimum of 150 mg of fibrinogen, although most bags typically contain around 250 mg, which is the value often used in clinical calculations. Additionally, each bag must contain at least 80 international units (IU) of factor VIII. Cryoprecipitate is indicated for use in the following clinical scenarios: Haemophilia: It is used as an emergency backup treatment when specific factor concentrates are unavailable. Von Willebrand’s disease: It can be administered to manage bleeding associated with this condition. Hypofibrinogenaemia: This refers to low fibrinogen levels, which can occur in situations such as massive transfusions. Bleeding due to excessive anticoagulation: While plasma, which contains most coagulation factors, is generally a better option for rapidly reversing anticoagulation, cryoprecipitate may be used in certain cases. Massive haemorrhage: Although red blood cells and volume expanders are typically more effective in managing massive blood loss, cryoprecipitate may be used in specific circumstances. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC): Cryoprecipitate can be utilized to address the coagulopathy associated with this condition.
